structure.title: Empirical Strategy (RD Design and DD Design)
Impacts of RGGVY: First Stage and Reduced-Form Economic Outcomes
Economic Impacts of Electrification: Rescaled (IV) Treatment Effects

observations.statement: States a sharp RD design at RGGVY's habitation-population eligibility threshold, using single-habitation villages so that observed village population proxies the unobserved habitation population that actually determined program eligibility.

Names two RD identifying assumptions explicitly: continuity of covariates and unobservables across the threshold, which is called fundamentally untestable, and non-manipulability of the running variable, argued to hold because eligibility used census population recorded years before the program was announced.

Frames the DD design as complementary to the RD design: it uses district-level variation from RGGVY's staggered two-wave rollout and requires a parallel-trends assumption, in exchange for covering villages of all sizes rather than only those near the eligibility cutoff.

States that parallel trends is assumed to hold only after conditioning on three sets of linear trends meant to absorb selection of districts into RGGVY's first wave: within-state expenditure-quartile trends, national expenditure-decile trends, and state-specific trends.

Defends the exclusion restriction for the DD-IV and fuzzy-RD scaling exercises institutionally: RGGVY prohibited hiring local workers and outcome data were collected years after most first-wave projects finished, so eligibility is argued to affect outcomes only through electrification itself.

Restricts the RD sample to villages consisting of exactly one habitation, identified by linking census villages to a separate habitation census, because subvillage habitation populations (the true eligibility unit) are otherwise unobserved.

Drops states lacking reliable 2001 village shapefiles from the RD sample because the nighttime-brightness control requires polygon-level matching, while the DD sample retains these states since its fixed-effects specification does not rely on a pre-period brightness control.

Presents a pre-program summary-statistics table comparing village-level covariates across nested samples (all districts, first-wave districts, and the final RD sample) alongside district-level pretrend regressions, to argue the RD sample resembles the broader population near the threshold.

Restricts the RD analysis to first-wave districts, where the eligibility threshold applied at the habitation level, explaining that the second wave's lower threshold left too little density of villages nearby for reliable inference and that focusing on the first wave lets outcomes be measured over a longer post-treatment horizon.

Builds the household DD analysis from a repeated cross-section of three national household-survey waves, collapsed to a district-year panel using survey sampling weights, because the survey lacks the village identifiers needed for the RD design.

Defines the preferred village-level welfare outcome as per capita consumption expenditure from a village-level dataset combining household-survey microdata with an independent household-development survey, chosen as described as the only source covering expenditure for the full universe of villages.

Constructs nighttime brightness as the maximum satellite pixel value within each village's shapefile polygon, removing year-specific measurement error via linear projection and dropping a small number of extreme outliers.

Defines the RD running variable as 2001 census village population, used as a proxy for the unobserved habitation population that legally determined RGGVY eligibility, valid only within the single-habitation subsample.

Rescales each endogenous 'full electrification' treatment variable (commercial power hours, nighttime brightness, household connection share) by a distributional benchmark, such as an interquartile shift or a move from no household connections to full connection, so IV estimates can be interpreted against a common full-electrification counterfactual.

Defines the household-survey expenditure outcome net of spending on electricity itself, so that it captures both the benefits and the costs of consuming power rather than mechanically rising with electricity purchases.

Reports, for each outcome column of the main RD electricity-access table, the point estimate with its standard error, the optimal bandwidth, the count of village observations, and the mean of the dependent variable among below-threshold villages, while fixed effects and controls are described once in the table note rather than varied across columns.

Reports a single treatment coefficient per outcome column in the district-level DD tables, together with the dependent-variable mean and the number of clusters, while the full control set (three linear-trend groups) and the clustering rule are described once in the table note.

Reports the first-stage coefficient, its standard error, and a weak-instrument F-statistic directly beneath each two-stage-least-squares column of the DD-IV table, alongside village-population percentiles for the size subsample used in that column.
Reports heteroskedasticity-robust nearest-neighbor standard errors for RD tables as the rdrobust default, without an explicit main-text discussion of why clustering was not applied to this design.

Clusters DD standard errors at the district level, the level at which RGGVY treatment (wave assignment) was determined, with an explicit rule for collapsing certain split or multi-district cases into a single cluster.

Clusters the village-level nighttime-brightness DD event study at a finer geographic block level than the district-level treatment assignment used elsewhere in the DD analysis, without a stated rationale in the main text for departing from assignment-level clustering in this specification.
Aggregates outcomes into indexed and combined measures in one panel of the reduced-form RD table, described by the authors as addressing concerns about testing many separate outcomes.

States explicitly, for the pooled DD-IV specification, that the first-stage F-statistic clears an informal rule-of-thumb threshold but falls short of a stricter weak-instrument critical value from the literature, reporting both the informal and formal benchmarks side by side.
Presents a density plot of the running variable around the eligibility threshold in the main text, to argue against manipulation or bunching in village population near the cutoff.
Assesses covariate balance across the RD threshold in an online appendix section not included in the main article, summarized in the main text as showing smoothness of pre-program covariates.

Reports first-stage electricity-access results by end-use sector and by extensive/intensive margin in a main-text RD table, with a companion appendix table repeating the exercise using the DD design to extend beyond the RD bandwidth.

Shows pre-trend evidence for nighttime brightness both as year-by-year RD coefficients before and after program announcement and as a DD event-study figure, both reported as showing no differential brightness before treatment.

Reports falsification checks in the online appendix, including RD estimates on samples where the threshold should not apply, RD estimates against a distribution of randomly generated placebo cutoffs, and a DD test that scrambles district treatment assignment.

Summarizes first-stage RD sensitivity to alternative kernels, bandwidth algorithms, standard errors, fixed effects, polynomial orders and sample criteria in a pair of online appendix figures rather than in the main text.

Shows the DD results are robust to dropping districts that either had projects spanning both program waves or had no RGGVY projects at all, a check reported in a footnote pointing to an appendix table.
Re-estimates the main household DD specification without its state-specific linear trends in an appendix table, checking that results are not an artifact of that particular detrending choice.

Repeats the internal-rate-of-return welfare calculations under an alternative, lower fixed-cost norm and under a no-population-growth assumption, summarizing both variants in dedicated appendix tables alongside the preferred specification.

States in the note of nearly every reduced-form RD and DD table that results are broadly robust to alternative kernels, bandwidth algorithms, controls and standard errors, with the full sensitivity analysis reported in appendix figures and tables rather than reproduced in the main tables.

Splits the DD-IV household analysis by within-year quintiles of survey sampling weights, used as a proxy for village population size, to separately estimate full-electrification effects for smaller versus larger villages.

Restricts a separate heterogeneity analysis to districts where RGGVY treated a high share of eligible villages, addressing a concern that scaling reduced-form estimates up to a full-electrification benchmark could extrapolate beyond the range of implementation intensity actually observed.
Plots firm-count and firm-employment DD effects separately across bins of baseline village population, to examine whether structural transformation through firm growth differs by village size.

Offers evidence of firm and firm-employment growth concentrated in larger villages as suggestive, explicitly labeled as such, evidence that structural transformation helps explain why welfare gains from electrification differ by village size.

Constructs, beyond the expenditure-based welfare estimates, a second model-guided welfare measure using a discrete/continuous household demand framework to compute consumer surplus from electricity consumption, cross-checking the two welfare approaches against each other.

Tests for crowd-out of pre-existing self-generated (diesel) power using fuel-purchase survey data, to rule out the alternative explanation that grid electrification merely displaced off-grid consumption rather than adding net power use, and reports the test in a footnote.

Interprets null intent-to-treat expenditure effects through the upper bound of the confidence interval expressed as a share of the baseline mean, rather than through the point estimate alone, to characterize how large an effect can be statistically ruled out.

Translates estimated nighttime-brightness effects into an implied number of newly lit households or connections by benchmarking against ground-truthing relationships reported in separate remote-sensing studies from other countries.

Expresses welfare returns from full electrification as multi-year internal rates of return and compares them against a standard cost-effectiveness threshold used elsewhere in development-finance practice, rather than leaving the returns as an unanchored number.

Compares point estimates for larger villages qualitatively to IV estimates from an earlier South African electrification study, to argue that the magnitude of the estimated positive effect is plausible relative to the existing literature.

Notes as a limitation that nighttime-brightness data cannot distinguish street lighting from broader household and enterprise electrification, addressing it only by citing the institutional fact that the program did not fund streetlights during the study wave.

Flags that the preferred village-level expenditure measure cannot be adjusted to remove electricity spending the way the household-survey measure can, so the RD-based welfare estimate may somewhat overstate net benefits relative to the DD-based one.

Distinguishes the RD estimates, local to villages near the eligibility threshold and representing a complier-type average effect, from the DD estimates, described as covering villages across the full population-size distribution.

Argues the setting generalizes to current electrification efforts by comparing the study country's income level during the sample period to income levels in countries with large unelectrified populations today, using this comparison to motivate external relevance rather than as a formal test.
Pairs each headline RD regression table with a binned-scatterplot RD figure generated from the same specification, relegating additional plots for less central outcomes to the appendix.
Presents DD event-study estimates as coefficient plots with confidence-interval whiskers rather than as full event-time coefficient tables in the main text.

Marks conventional significance levels with asterisks in regression tables while also reporting an explicit confidence interval alongside each point estimate, communicating precision in two complementary ways even for null results.
Presents a dedicated pre-program summary-statistics table, split into village-level and district-level panels, before any treatment-effect results are shown.

Previews the first-stage, reduced-form, and IV-rescaled welfare results in sequence within the introduction, before any empirical section, then closes the introduction with an explicit paragraph enumerating the paper's contributions to the literature.

Places the empirical strategy section before the data section, and pushes detailed robustness and diagnostic material into online appendices referenced by letter and number rather than into a separate main-text robustness section.

Structurally separates intent-to-treat 'impacts of the program' results from IV-rescaled 'economic impacts of electrification' results into two distinct numbered sections, signaling that the rescaling exercise is conceptually downstream of the main program-evaluation results.

Includes a dedicated data-availability statement at the end of the article citing a named public repository entry, with a persistent identifier, as containing all data and programs needed to replicate the paper.

observations.statement: Explicitly names the statistical software framework used for the RD implementation, attributing it to its original methodological source, rather than leaving the estimation routine unspecified.
observations.quote: rdrobust framework developed by Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik

observations.statement: Combines publicly available census and satellite sources with administrative and survey microdata obtained through research access arrangements (a poverty-targeting census subset and firm-level economic census records), without describing a step-by-step access procedure for the latter in the main text.

concordance.paper_says: Sharp RD implemented via the rdrobust framework (Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik 2014) with a triangular kernel, MSE-optimal bandwidth, and heteroskedasticity-robust nearest-neighbor standard errors; a fuzzy-RD variant instruments for electrification.
concordance.card_shows: s1.estimator = local_polynomial_rd, s1.command = rdrobust, s1.package = rdrobust.

concordance.paper_says: Main RD specification (equation 1) includes state fixed effects and controls for pre-program covariates including the lagged outcome variable where available.
concordance.card_shows: s1.fixed_effects is null; the card records no fixed-effects value for this specification.

concordance.paper_says: RD standard errors are described as heteroskedasticity-robust nearest-neighbor standard errors from the rdrobust default, with no clustering mentioned for this design.
DD and DD-IV standard errors are clustered at the district level, the level of RGGVY treatment assignment, with a stated rule for collapsing split-district clusters.
concordance.card_shows: s2.se.type = cluster and s3.se.type = cluster, but s2.se.cluster_level and s3.se.cluster_level are both null in the card.

concordance.paper_says: Main DD specification (equation 2) includes district and year fixed effects plus three sets of linear trends meant to absorb selection of districts into RGGVY's first wave.
concordance.card_shows: s2.fixed_effects is null; the card records only a bound local-macro value ('pca01_id year#stdt') for one fixed-effects variant, not the full specification described in the paper.

concordance.paper_says: RD bandwidths are chosen via an MSE-optimal procedure computed separately for each outcome variable, following a specific bandwidth-selection method from the RD literature.
concordance.card_shows: Diagnostic x2 (bandwidth_selection) records the mserd bandwidth-selection option as an author-stated observation, matching the paper.

concordance.paper_says: RD sample is restricted to single-habitation villages in first-wave districts with reliable population and lights measurements, excluding cases with large population or lights mismatches.
concordance.card_shows: pipeline.sample_restrictions records matching restriction logic (single-habitation, first-wave, population/lights quality filters) tied to specification s1.

concordance.paper_says: Analysis combines two censuses, a poverty-targeting census subset, a village expenditure dataset, an economic census of firms, school records, satellite nighttime lights, and a national household survey.
concordance.card_shows: The card's data[] array records census, geospatial, NSS household-survey, Economic Census and SECC entries as data types, largely without names, access terms or periods filled in.

concordance.paper_says: A first-stage weak-instrument F-statistic is reported for each DD-IV column and compared against both an informal rule-of-thumb and a formal weak-instrument critical value from the literature.
concordance.card_shows: Diagnostic x1 (first_stage) has status 'unknown' with no recorded observation or evidence in the card.

concordance.paper_says: RD density/manipulation tests and multiple falsification exercises (wrong-cutoff samples, randomized placebo cutoffs, scrambled DD assignment) are reported, mostly in the online appendix.
concordance.card_shows: The card's diagnostics list contains only first_stage, bandwidth_selection and polynomial_order entries; no density-test or placebo-test diagnostic is recorded.

concordance.paper_says: DD robustness checks include alternative bandwidths around the eligibility threshold and a heterogeneous-effects specification interacting treatment with baseline power-supply hours.
concordance.card_shows: robustness[0] (alt_bandwidth) and robustness[1] (alt_fixed_effects) are both tied to specification s2 with relationship_status 'unresolved' and no variant specification ids recorded.

concordance.paper_says: The paper presents nine numbered main-text tables and nine main-text figures covering first-stage, reduced-form, rescaled, heterogeneity and welfare results, plus many appendix tables and figures.
concordance.card_shows: outputs.tables records only two table entries (table_rd_vdelec.tex and table_diff_in_disc_vdelec.tex) and no figures, reflecting the card's minimal-coverage reading rather than the paper's full output set.

gaps: No preregistration, IRB approval, or informed-consent statement appears anywhere in the main text; the study relies entirely on secondary administrative, census, satellite and survey data rather than a fielded experiment, so a preregistration/ethics statement may not be applicable.

No explicit justification is given in the main text for why RD standard errors are left unclustered while DD standard errors are clustered by district; the RD choice appears to follow the rdrobust default rather than a stated design argument.
R-squared is not reported in the main RD or DD regression tables (rdrobust and reghdfe-style output favors bandwidth, cluster count and dependent-variable mean instead).

Appendices A, B and C are referenced dozens of times for balance tables, full robustness batteries, falsification tests and additional outcomes, but are described as available only online and are not included in this text extraction, so their exact content could not be verified beyond the main text's own summaries.
The main text does not describe a step-by-step access procedure for the restricted low-income SECC subset or the Economic Census microdata, beyond naming them as administrative/survey sources.

reading.note: Read the full extracted text of all 36 pages, covering the abstract, introduction, institutional background, empirical strategy (RD and DD designs), data, first-stage and reduced-form results, IV-rescaled economic-impact and welfare analysis, conclusion, data-availability statement and reference list. The paper's online Appendices A-C, referenced repeatedly for balance tests, falsification tests and detailed robustness tables, are a separate document not included in this text extraction and were not read; their existence and the authors' summaries of their content are recorded only as stated in the main text.
